title: All things to all people (1 Corinthians 9:19–27)
hookLine: Paul bends every habit to reach people, and runs one straight course
tomorrow: Paul promises a way out of every temptation. where's the door?

cards: Three texts in one minute. To your grandmother: full sentences, punctuation, a heart at the end. To your little cousin: one emoji.
To the team chat: a picture and nothing else. Same person, three keyboards.

Paul does something like that with whole towns of people, and then he writes a sentence with a knot in it: "For though I be free from all men, yet have I made myself servant unto all, that I might gain the more."
Free from everyone. Servant to everyone. How can both be true?

teach.h: FREE FROM ALL, SERVANT TO ALL.
teach.b: Paul untangles it with a list. "Unto the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews." To those outside the law, he lives as one outside it, though he adds that he is still "under the law to Christ."
"To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak: I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some." So the knot loosens. His freedom is what lets him serve.
Nobody owns him, so he can give up his rights, his menu, his place at the table. And notice the last word. Not all.
Some. Then, with no warning, he's at the stadium. "Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain."
Athletes, he says, are "temperate in all things" for a crown that fades.
"I therefore so run, not as uncertainly; so fight I, not as one that beateth the air." No drifting off the track.
No punching at nothing. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: the man who bends for everyone keeps exactly one person on a strict course, himself. What bends is the habit.
What stays put is the reason: "this I do for the gospel's sake."

how: Some Christians who serve in another culture point to 1 Corinthians 9 as they learn its language and customs, and the runner's verses are read at some Christian gatherings for athletes.

games.q: what does “all things to all people” mean?
o: agreeing with whatever each person believes
bending your habits to reach each person
trying to be everyone's favorite at once

games.q: all things to all people — tap the pairs.
p: they which run in a race
run all, but one receiveth the prize

s: all things to all people means telling each crowd what it wants to hear
Paul bends his habits, not his reason: this I do for the gospel's sake.
Paul says he became all things to all men to save everyone
his last word is some: that I might by all means save some.
Paul pictures himself as a runner and a fighter in the same breath
so run, not as uncertainly; so fight I, not as one that beateth the air.

games.q: you join a new team where everyone stays after practice to stretch and talk. you usually leave the minute it ends. what fits Paul's way?
o: stay and stretch with them, and keep your own values.
leave as usual; changing habits for people is fake.
copy everything they do, even what you think is wrong.
games.why: Paul gives up habits and rights to reach people, but not his course: so run, not as uncertainly. bending a habit isn't bending yourself.

practice: Bring to mind one person whose ways aren't yours: how they talk, eat, pray, or spend a Saturday. Name one habit of yours you could set down to meet them on their ground, and the one thing in you that wouldn't move.
Then let your breath run steady, like a runner who knows the course.

wordCard.voice: All things to all people. Paul bends his habits to reach each person, and keeps his own life on one course.

orig.note: Greek: to all I have become all things.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: so run, not as uncertainly and not beating the air. See you tomorrow.
